name: Dark Sienna
lede: Dark Sienna pushes the earth pigment sienna almost to black-red, and it is one of the most common colors in our entire painting archive.

sections.title: An earth pigment, darkened
sections.body: The name follows the usual grammar for our [1]. Sienna itself is a natural iron-oxide earth pigment named for Siena, Italy, and English sources first use it as a color word around 1760 [1]. In Japan the same earthy hue family is called *Taisha-iro*, 代赭色, literally "red ochre color" [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 classifies Dark Sienna as a dark reddish brown, and Wikipedia's own citation for the color traces back to that same system [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[black-bean]] and [[dusty-oxblood]], at 4.1 and 5.2 ΔE [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Dark Sienna appears in 5.16 percent of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, 1,227 of them as photographed, more common than 86 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1500s, found in 5.2 percent of the 2,231 paintings from that century, 1.6 times its own museums' baseline [3]. Inside a painting it most often serves as a hidden color, in 46 percent of its 692 clearest appearances, buried in shadow rather than shown on the surface [3].

[[painter:john-singer-sargent|Sargent]] uses it most by raw count, in 7 of his 287 works here, though no single painter stands out against the museum baseline the way some do for rarer colors [3]. It shares canvases with Blood Red and Deep Red far more than chance, with lifts of 8.2 and 6.6 [3]. The earliest match is dated 1210, a plausible age for an earth pigment that painters have ground for millennia, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. It sits deep in the [[brown]] family, far too red to pass for plain grey [3].
